subject: ela
skillName: Ask and answer questions about a speaker

items.prompt:
A speaker says: 'Many animals are endangered because of habitat loss.' A student is not sure what 'habitat loss' means. Which is the BEST clarifying question?
A) 'Do you like animals?'
B) 'What does habitat loss mean, and how does it endanger animals?'
C) 'Which animals are your favorites?'
items.answer: B) 'What does habitat loss mean, and how does it endanger animals?'

steps: The student is confused by the term 'habitat loss' and wants to understand how it connects to endangerment.
Option A and C are personal questions unrelated to clarifying the statement.
Option B asks for two things: the definition AND the connection — this fully clarifies the statement.

items.prompt:
A teacher says: 'Thomas Edison invented many things.' After the talk, a student asks: 'You said Edison invented many things — can you name the most important one?' Why is this a strong question?
A) It is not strong — it asks for an opinion
B) It gathers specific additional information by asking for the most important example from the speaker's statement
C) It changes the topic to opinions about inventions
items.answer: B) It gathers specific additional information by asking for the most important example from the speaker's statement

steps: The teacher said 'many things' without specifying what they were.
The student's question stays on topic and asks for the most important example — gathering specific information.
While 'most important' could involve some judgment, it is asking the speaker to prioritize and explain, which gathers information.

items.prompt:
A speaker says: 'The brain controls everything your body does.' A student asks: 'Does the brain control things you do without thinking, like breathing?' Identify what type of question this is.
A) A question that changes the topic
B) A question that deepens understanding by exploring the limits of the statement
C) A question that disagrees with the speaker
items.answer: B) A question that deepens understanding by exploring the limits of the statement

steps: The statement says the brain controls 'everything'.
The student is testing that claim: does 'everything' include automatic actions like breathing?
This question deepens understanding by exploring the scope of the speaker's claim.
It is not a disagreement — it is a thoughtful exploration of the meaning.

items.prompt:
A classmate presents about recycling and says: 'Recycling saves energy. You should recycle.' After the presentation, which question gathers the MOST additional useful information?
A) 'How much energy does recycling actually save?'
B) 'Do you recycle at your house?'
C) 'What is your favorite color?'
items.answer: A) 'How much energy does recycling actually save?'

steps: The classmate said recycling 'saves energy' without specifying how much.
Option A asks for specific quantitative information that makes the claim more concrete.
Option B is a personal question about the speaker's habits — not about the topic's information.
Option C is completely off topic.

items.prompt:
A speaker says: 'Monarch butterflies migrate thousands of miles.' A student asks: 'Where do they start and where do they end up?' Is this a good question?
A) No — the speaker already answered this
B) Yes — the speaker mentioned migration but did not specify the route; this gathers additional information
C) No — the distance was already given
items.answer: B) Yes — the speaker mentioned migration but did not specify the route; this gathers additional information

steps: The speaker said 'thousands of miles' but did not say WHERE the butterflies start or end.
The student's question asks for additional information: the start and end points of the migration.
This is a strong follow-up question that fills in details the speaker omitted.

items.prompt:
A student hears a speaker say: 'Scientists believe there may be life on other planets.' The student asks: 'What evidence do scientists have that makes them believe that?' What is the purpose of this question?
A) To ask for evidence that supports the speaker's claim — deepening understanding
B) To argue that the speaker is wrong
C) To change the topic to space travel
items.answer: A) To ask for evidence that supports the speaker's claim — deepening understanding

steps: The speaker made a claim ('scientists believe...') without providing evidence.
Asking for evidence deepens understanding of WHY scientists think this.
This is a high-quality comprehension question that asks the speaker to support their statement.

items.prompt:
A teacher explains a concept and a student feels she understood it. A classmate asks a question the student had not thought of. After hearing the answer, the student says: 'Oh! I did not know that.' What does this show?
A) The student was not paying attention
B) Questions from others can deepen understanding even for students who thought they understood
C) The student should have asked more questions earlier
items.answer: B) Questions from others can deepen understanding even for students who thought they understood

steps: This scenario shows that asking good questions benefits the whole group.
Even students who feel they understood a topic can learn more when others ask probing questions.
This is one of the values of collaborative listening: questions from one person help everyone.

items.prompt:
A speaker says: 'Sharks have been on Earth for over 400 million years.' A student asks: 'Does that mean sharks were alive when dinosaurs were alive?' What type of question is this?
A) A question that asks for evidence
B) A question that makes a connection to deepen understanding
C) A question that changes the subject to dinosaurs
items.answer: B) A question that makes a connection to deepen understanding

steps: The student connects the 400-million-year figure to their knowledge of when dinosaurs lived.
Asking 'does that mean sharks were alive with dinosaurs?' explores a connection, deepening understanding of the timeframe.
This is not changing the subject — it directly uses the speaker's information to ask a logical follow-up.

items.prompt:
A student answers a question about what a speaker said. The student's answer is: 'I think the speaker said rainforests are important.' What is missing from a strong answer?
A) 'I think' should be replaced with a specific detail: 'The speaker said rainforests are important BECAUSE they produce oxygen and are home to millions of species'
B) The word 'rainforests' should not be used
C) The student should have started with 'In my opinion'
items.answer: A) 'I think' should be replaced with a specific detail: 'The speaker said rainforests are important BECAUSE they produce oxygen and are home to millions of species'

steps: A strong answer about what a speaker said uses specific details from what was actually spoken.
'I think' signals uncertainty — a better answer states specifically what was said.
Including WHY (the reason: oxygen production, species habitat) shows the student understood the key information.
Specific details prove the student listened carefully.

items.prompt:
A student is asked: 'What did the speaker say about the importance of sleep?' The student answers: 'The speaker said kids need 9–11 hours of sleep because sleep helps the brain process information and the body repair itself.' Is this a strong answer?
A) No — the student included too much information
B) Yes — the answer includes the specific recommendation (9–11 hours) and two reasons given by the speaker
C) No — the student should have said less
items.answer: B) Yes — the answer includes the specific recommendation (9–11 hours) and two reasons given by the speaker

steps: A strong answer about what a speaker said includes specific facts AND the reasons behind them.
The student gave the specific quantity (9–11 hours) and two reasons: brain processing and body repair.
This demonstrates careful listening and accurate recall of the speaker's key points.

items.prompt:
A speaker talks about ocean pollution. A student wants to understand the most important part. Which question best targets comprehension of the speaker's central point?
A) 'What did you think was the single most important thing you wanted us to know?'
B) 'What did you eat for lunch?'
C) 'Is the ocean near your house?'
items.answer: A) 'What did you think was the single most important thing you wanted us to know?'

steps: This question asks the speaker to identify their central message — clarifying what the listener should take away.
It is a meta-question about the speaker's purpose, which deepens comprehension of the whole talk.
Options B and C are personal and unrelated to the content.

items.prompt:
A teacher explains: 'Gravity keeps everything on the ground.' A student asks: 'If gravity keeps things on the ground, how do airplanes fly?' Is this a good question?
A) No — airplanes are a different topic
B) Yes — the student notices an apparent contradiction and asks for clarification that deepens understanding
C) No — the student is showing off
items.answer: B) Yes — the student notices an apparent contradiction and asks for clarification that deepens understanding

steps: The teacher said gravity keeps everything on the ground, but airplanes clearly fly.
The student is asking the teacher to explain how this apparent contradiction is resolved.
This is a sophisticated clarifying question that probes the limits of the statement.
The answer (thrust and lift overcome gravity) deepens understanding of both gravity and flight.

items.prompt:
After a speaker's talk, a student gives this answer to a question: 'The speaker said that the rainforest has four layers, and each layer has different plants and animals.' What does this answer demonstrate?
A) The student was not listening carefully
B) The student listened carefully and can accurately describe a specific detail from the speaker's talk
C) The student made up information
items.answer: B) The student listened carefully and can accurately describe a specific detail from the speaker's talk

steps: The student's answer includes a specific detail (four layers) and a related idea (each has different plants/animals).
This level of detail can only come from careful listening.
Accurately recounting what a speaker said is exactly what this standard measures.

items.prompt:
A speaker gives a presentation about space. At the end, she asks: 'Any questions?' A student asks: 'I understood most of your talk, but I was confused about why black holes are called black. Can you explain that part again?' Is this a good clarifying question?
A) No — the student should not admit confusion
B) Yes — the student identified a specific point of confusion and asked the speaker to explain it again
C) No — black holes were probably not in the talk
items.answer: B) Yes — the student identified a specific point of confusion and asked the speaker to explain it again

steps: Admitting confusion and asking for clarification is a strong listening skill — not a weakness.
The student named the specific part they didn't understand (why they are called black).
Asking a speaker to explain something again is an appropriate and useful clarifying question.

items.prompt:
A speaker says: 'Reading every day makes you smarter.' A student asks: 'Is that true for any kind of reading, or does it have to be books?' What kind of question is this?
A) A question that gathers additional information by exploring the scope of the speaker's claim
B) An off-topic question about books vs. other reading
C) A disagreement with the speaker
items.answer: A) A question that gathers additional information by exploring the scope of the speaker's claim

steps: The speaker said 'reading every day' without specifying what type of reading.
The student's question explores the boundaries of the claim: does it apply to all reading or just books?
This gathers additional information about the conditions of the speaker's statement.
It does not disagree — it asks for clarification of scope.
